claim: Protein expression levels are optimized to maximize the fitness of organisms, determined by demand and constraint.
source: Expression levels of proteins are optimized to maximize the fitness of organisms, and the evolutionary principle that determines those levels is considered to be demand and constraint (Bruggeman et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruggeman et al., 2020 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Demand is the evolutionary pressure that works to increase protein expression to meet functional requirements.
source: Demand is the evolutionary pressure that works to increase the expression of a protein to meet the requirements of its function
evidence: Definition provided in the manuscript as part of the theoretical framework

claim: Constraint is the evolutionary pressure that works to decrease protein expression to avoid negative effects of excess protein.
source: constraint is the evolutionary pressure that works to decrease the expression of a protein to avoid the negative effects produced by excess protein.
evidence: Definition provided in the manuscript as part of the theoretical framework

claim: Constraints appear as disturbances in cellular function when protein is overexpressed.
source: Constraints appear as disturbances in cellular function when the protein is overexpressed (Figure 1A, the red arrow).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the relationship

claim: The mechanisms of constraining expression levels can be classified into four major categories: resource overload, stoichiometry imbalance, pathway modulation, and promiscuous interaction.
source: The mechanisms of constraining expression levels, or defects due to overexpression, can be roughly classified into four major categories (Moriya, 2015; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moriya, 2015 and reference to Figure 1B

claim: Resource overload is a disorder in which intracellular resources used for protein processing are depleted or monopolized.
source: 'Resource overload' (also called 'burden'; Kastberg et al., 2022) is a disorder in which intracellular resources used for protein processing, such as synthesis, localization, degradation, and modification of proteins, are depleted or monopolized by the processing of that protein, resulting in a disruption of processing of other proteins (Dong et al., 1995; Eguchi et al., 2018; Kintaka et al., 2020; Kintaka et al., 2016; Stoebel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Resource overload occurs in proteins with high expression levels.
source: This phenomenon occurs in proteins with high expression levels.
evidence: Statement about when resource overload occurs

claim: Stoichiometry imbalance is a disorder triggered by an imbalance of amounts between constituents within complexes.
source: 'Stoichiometry imbalance' is a disorder triggered by an imbalance of amounts between constituents within complexes, leading to untimely activation or inactivation (pathway modulation), degradation (resource overload), aggregation (promiscuous interaction), etc. (Kaizu et al., 2010; Makanae et al., 2013; Papp et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaizu et al., 2010; Makanae et al., 2013; Papp et al., 2003

claim: Stoichiometry imbalance occurs due to overexpression of proteins that form complexes.
source: This occurs due to the overexpression of proteins that form complexes.
evidence: Statement about when stoichiometry imbalance occurs

claim: Pathway modulation is a disorder in which pathways are untimely activated or inactivated.
source: 'Pathway modulation' is a disorder in which pathways are untimely activated or inactivated. This occurs especially with overexpression of proteins involved in pathway regulation, such as metabolic enzymes, kinases and phosphatases, and transcription factors (Prelich, 2012; Youn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prelich, 2012; Youn et al., 2017

claim: Promiscuous interaction is a disorder in which weak interactions are enhanced by mass action to form complexes or aggregates that are not normally formed.
source: 'Promiscuous interaction' is a disorder in which weak interactions are enhanced by mass action to form complexes or aggregates that are not normally formed. This damages cellular function by inactivating essential proteins or overloading degradation resources and is caused by overexpression of intrinsically disordered proteins or liquid-liquid phase-separating proteins (Bolognesi et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2010; Vavouri et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bolognesi et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2010; Vavouri et al., 2009

claim: The synthesis process, which processes all proteins, should have the largest capacity among protein processing processes.
source: Essentially, the synthesis, in which all proteins are processed, should have the largest capacity, while processes such as transport, folding, and degradation, in which only a fraction of proteins are processed, should have smaller capacities.
evidence: Logical inference based on the barrel model presented in Figure 1C

claim: Adding transport or degradation signals to a cytosolic protein lowers the expression limit.
source: In fact, adding transport or degradation signals to a cytosolic protein lowers the expression limit (Kintaka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kintaka et al., 2016

claim: The final constraint barrier that emerges when all possible constraints are removed is the overloading of the synthesis process.
source: In that light, the final constraint barrier that emerges when all possible constraints are removed is the overloading of the synthesis process.
evidence: Logical inference from the barrel model and previous observations

claim: Overloading of the synthesis process is specifically referred to as 'protein burden' or 'protein cost'.
source: Overloading of the synthesis process is specifically referred to as 'protein burden' or 'protein cost' (Eguchi et al., 2018; Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eguchi et al., 2018; Kafri et al., 2016

claim: The idea of protein burden was first proposed in studies of the cost of unnecessary induction of the lac operon in Escherichia coli.
source: This idea was first proposed in studies of the cost of unnecessary induction of the lac operon in Escherichia coli (Koch, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koch, 1983

claim: During protein burden, depletion of materials, machinery, and factors necessary for transcription and translation occurs.
source: During protein burden, it is presumed that depletion of the materials, machinery, and factors necessary for transcription and translation occurs, along with competition from these monopolies.
evidence: Statement about presumed mechanisms of protein burden

claim: Amino acids and aminoacyl-tRNAs are major candidates for depletion during protein burden.
source: In particular, amino acids and aminoacyl-tRNAs are major candidates for depletion (Kastberg et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kastberg et al., 2022

claim: Ribosomes have been considered major candidates for depletion during protein burden.
source: In addition, ribosomes, which are crucial for protein synthesis, themselves require significant resources for their synthesis and have therefore been considered major candidates for depletion during protein burden, as they compete for these limited resources (Metzl-Raz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Metzl-Raz et al., 2017

claim: Transcription is rate-limiting in phosphate starvation and translation in nitrogen source starvation during protein burden in budding yeast.
source: Mechanistic analysis of protein burden in budding yeast, a model eukaryotic cell, has been intensively conducted by Barkai and colleagues, who reported that transcription is rate-limiting in phosphate starvation and translation in nitrogen source starvation (Kafri et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kafri et al., 2016

claim: Basic transcription factors are limiting resources during protein burden in yeast.
source: and that basic transcription factors are limiting resources (Metzl-Raz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Metzl-Raz et al., 2020

claim: A cellular response to protein burden includes increased cell size and enhanced protein synthesis capacity.
source: In addition, a cellular response in the form of increased cell size and enhanced protein synthesis capacity has been observed (Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kafri et al., 2016

claim: The previously expected decrease in ribosomes during protein burden has not been detected.
source: Thus, the previously expected decrease in ribosomes has not been detected.
evidence: Statement about what has not been observed in previous studies

claim: Model proteins selected for protein burden studies in yeast include fluorescent proteins and certain glycolytic enzymes.
source: Model proteins selected in this manner in yeast include fluorescent proteins (FPs) and certain glycolytic enzymes (Eguchi et al., 2018; Farkas et al., 2018; Kafri et al., 2016; Kintaka et al., 2016; Kintaka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Fluorescent proteins do not have a specific function or interaction partner in yeast cells and are not actively sorted into cellular compartments other than the cytosol.
source: FPs do not have a specific function or interaction partner in yeast cells and are not actively sorted into cellular compartments other than the cytosol.
evidence: Statement about properties of fluorescent proteins in yeast

claim: Glycolytic enzymes are naturally expressed at very high levels and are considered to be less constrained.
source: On the other hand, glycolytic enzymes are naturally expressed at very high levels and are thus considered to be less constrained.
evidence: Statement about properties of glycolytic enzymes

claim: Fluorescent proteins and glycolytic enzymes exhibit an expression limit of approximately 15% of total protein in yeast cells.
source: Notably, these proteins exhibit an expression limit of approximately 15% of total protein in yeast cells (Eguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eguchi et al., 2018

claim: Enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) forms a chaperone-entrapped aggregate upon overexpression.
source: Indeed, the enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP), which we have used as a model for protein burden (Kintaka et al., 2020; Kintaka et al., 2016; Makanae et al., 2013), was found to form a chaperone-entrapped aggregate upon overexpression and trigger the heat shock response due to its low folding ability (Namba et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Namba et al., 2022

claim: EGFP overexpression triggers the heat shock response due to its low folding ability.
source: Indeed, the enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP), which we have used as a model for protein burden (Kintaka et al., 2020; Kintaka et al., 2016; Makanae et al., 2013), was found to form a chaperone-entrapped aggregate upon overexpression and trigger the heat shock response due to its low folding ability (Namba et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Namba et al., 2022

claim: EGFP overexpression causes abnormal yeast cell morphology through proteasomal stress because it contains cysteines.
source: Its overexpression also causes abnormal yeast cell morphology through proteasomal stress as it contains cysteines.
evidence: Statement about effects of EGFP overexpression

claim: MoxGFP (mox), which has improved folding properties and lacks cysteine residues, showed a higher expression limit than EGFP.
source: The moxGFP (mox), which improved folding properties and lacks cysteine residues (Costantini et al., 2015), showed a higher expression limit and no longer induced abnormal morphologies.
evidence: Supported by citation to Costantini et al., 2015 and comparison with EGFP

claim: MoxGFP overexpression no longer induces abnormal morphologies.
source: The moxGFP (mox), which improved folding properties and lacks cysteine residues (Costantini et al., 2015), showed a higher expression limit and no longer induced abnormal morphologies.
evidence: Statement about effects of moxGFP overexpression

claim: Even when overexpressing mox, the anticipated depletion and competition for factors, or cellular responses to them have not been observed.
source: However, even when overexpressing mox, the anticipated depletion and competition for factors, or cellular responses to them have not been observed (Namba et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Namba et al., 2022

claim: A mutation causing loss of fluorescence in mox and other fluorescent proteins increased the expression limit up to threefold, to more than 40% of total protein.
source: In this study, we found that a mutation causing loss of fluorescence in mox and other fluorescent proteins increased the expression limit up to threefold, to more than 40% of total protein.
evidence: Primary finding of the study

claim: Non-fluorescent mox (mox-YG) and enzymatically inactive Gpm1 (Gpm1–CCmut) are currently the least constrained proteins based on the neutrality index.
source: Introducing a neutrality index (NI) to assess protein constraint, we found that non-fluorescent mox (mox-YG) and enzymatically inactive Gpm1 (Gpm1–CCmut) are currently the least constrained.
evidence: Primary finding of the study using the neutrality index

claim: Mox-YG and Gpm1-CCmut can be expressed at levels exceeding 40% of total protein while maintaining yeast growth.
source: These proteins can be expressed at levels exceeding 40% of total protein while maintaining yeast growth.
evidence: Primary finding of the study

claim: The transcriptome of cells expressing mox-YG to the limit indicated that the cells were in a nitrogen source requirement state.
source: The transcriptome of cells expressing mox-YG to the limit indicated that the cells were in a nitrogen source requirement state.
evidence: Primary finding from transcriptome analysis

claim: Proteome analysis of mox-YG overexpressing cells revealed increased mitochondrial protein and decreased ribosome abundance.
source: Proteome analysis revealed increased mitochondrial protein and decreased ribosome abundance, similar to the inactivated state of the TORC1 pathway.
evidence: Primary finding from proteome analysis

claim: The proteome changes in mox-YG overexpressing cells are similar to the inactivated state of the TORC1 pathway.
source: Proteome analysis revealed increased mitochondrial protein and decreased ribosome abundance, similar to the inactivated state of the TORC1 pathway.
evidence: Comparison of proteome data with known TORC1 inactivation state

claim: The decrease in ribosome abundance in mox-YG overexpressing cells was presumably due to defective nucleolus formation.
source: The decrease in ribosome abundance was presumably due to defective nucleolus formation, partially rescued by a mutation in the nuclear exosome.
evidence: Inference from multiple observations including microscopy and genetic rescue

claim: A mutation in the nuclear exosome partially rescued the defective nucleolus formation in mox-YG overexpressing cells.
source: The decrease in ribosome abundance was presumably due to defective nucleolus formation, partially rescued by a mutation in the nuclear exosome.
evidence: Primary finding from genetic analysis

claim: Massive overexpression of excess protein (protein burden) causes nitrogen source starvation.
source: These findings suggest that massive overexpression of excess protein, termed protein burden, causes nitrogen source starvation, a metabolic shift toward more energy-efficient respiration, and a ribosomal biosynthesis defect due to an imbalance between ribosomal protein and rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from transcriptome and proteome data

claim: Massive overexpression of excess protein causes a metabolic shift toward more energy-efficient respiration.
source: These findings suggest that massive overexpression of excess protein, termed protein burden, causes nitrogen source starvation, a metabolic shift toward more energy-efficient respiration, and a ribosomal biosynthesis defect due to an imbalance between ribosomal protein and rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from proteome data and oxygen consumption measurements

claim: Massive overexpression of excess protein causes a ribosomal biosynthesis defect due to an imbalance between ribosomal protein and rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus.
source: These findings suggest that massive overexpression of excess protein, termed protein burden, causes nitrogen source starvation, a metabolic shift toward more energy-efficient respiration, and a ribosomal biosynthesis defect due to an imbalance between ribosomal protein and rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from proteome data, microscopy, and genetic rescue experiments

claim: Overexpression of fluorescent proteins and their YG mutants all caused growth inhibition.
source: Overexpression of the FPs and mutants all caused growth inhibition (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: EGFP and mox were expressed at about 15% of the total protein as previously reported.
source: EGFP and mox were expressed at about 15% of the total protein as previously reported (Kintaka et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kintaka et al., 2016 and current data

claim: mCherry and YG mutants were expressed at higher levels than EGFP and mox.
source: but mCherry (mChe) and YG mutants were expressed at higher levels.
evidence: Comparison of protein expression levels from SDS-PAGE data

claim: Mox-YG expressed 44% of the total protein.
source: Mox-YG expressed 44% of the total protein (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: The neutrality index (NI) is calculated as the product of %MGR and %protein level.
source: Here, we describe 'unconstrained' as 'neutral' and calculate the neutrality index (NI) as the product of %MGR and %protein level.
evidence: Definition of the neutrality index provided in the manuscript

claim: Introducing a non-fluorescent mutation in FPs uniformly increases neutrality.
source: The NI of each protein indicates that introducing a non-fluorescent mutation in FPs uniformly increases neutrality (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Having fluorescence is a constraint on the expression of fluorescent proteins.
source: suggesting that 'having fluorescence' is a constraint on the expression of FPs.
evidence: Inference from the observation that non-fluorescent mutations increase neutrality

claim: The most neutral proteins were sfGFP-YG and mox-YG, with NIs of about 2400.
source: The most neutral proteins were sfGFP-YG and mox-YG, with NIs of about 2400.
evidence: Supported by neutrality index calculations from experimental data

claim: sfGFP-YG and mox-YG have nearly identical NIs despite significant differences in growth inhibition and expression limits.
source: Notably, despite significant differences in the degree of growth inhibition and expression limits between the two proteins, their NIs are nearly identical (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F and G

claim: sfGFP-YG and mox-YG differ only in two amino acid residues (Cys - Ser).
source: They differ only in two amino acid residues (Cys - Ser; Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: The constraints indicated by NI are not affected by translation efficiency.
source: Thus, the constraints indicated by NI are apparently not affected by translation efficiency.
evidence: Inference from comparison of codon-optimized and non-optimized mCherry variants

claim: Cell enlargement is a phenomenon that occurs specifically when fluorescent mCherry is overexpressed.
source: Interestingly, the mChe-YG cells did not show enlargement (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A, B), indicating that cell enlargement is a phenomenon that occurs specifically when fluorescent mChe is overexpressed.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A, B

claim: The growth inhibition caused by overexpression of mox-YG is a burden on translation rather than on transcription.
source: It should be noted that the growth inhibition caused by the overexpression of mox-YG in this study is a burden on translation rather than on transcription. This is because overexpression of a frameshift mutant (moxFS), in which four nucleotides were inserted directly after the ATG of the mox-YG gene, abolished the notable growth delay (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C, D).
evidence: Supported by data from frameshift mutant experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C, D

claim: When yeast was grown in the dark, the degree of growth inhibition of mox was the same as in light.
source: When yeast was grown in the dark, the degree of growth inhibition of mox was the same (Figure 2—figure supplement 7A)
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7A

claim: The expression limit of mox was increased when grown in the dark.
source: and the expression limit of mox was rather increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: Supported by protein quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7B

claim: Phototoxicity exists when expressing mox with fluorescence.
source: Phototoxicity does indeed exist when expressing mox with fluorescence. This is because, when exposed to strong light, cells overexpressing mox show a reduced growth rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 7C–E) and abnormalities in their internal structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 7F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7C–F

claim: The expression limits of mox and mox-YG were almost unchanged by light exposure.
source: However, the expression limits of mox and mox-YG were almost unchanged by the light (Figure 2—figure supplement 7G, H).
evidence: Supported by protein quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7G, H

claim: The constraint on fluorescent protein expression was not due to phototoxicity itself.
source: Thus, the constraint was not due to phototoxicity itself.
evidence: Inference from the observation that expression limits were unchanged by light

claim: The number of Tyr residues was irrelevant to the constraint on fluorescent protein expression.
source: The number of Tyr residues was also irrelevant because NI was like that of mox-YG when a single Tyr was added to the C-terminus of mox-YG (Figure 2—figure supplement 8A–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8A–E

claim: When H2O2 was added to the medium, stronger growth inhibition occurred only in mox.
source: When H2O2 was added to the medium, stronger growth inhibition occurred only in mox (Figure 2—figure supplement 8F–H).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8F–H

claim: Mox-YG, like mox, was present throughout the cytoplasm and did not cause any characteristic localization or aggregation.
source: Mox-YG, like mox, was present throughout the cytoplasm and did not cause any characteristic localization or aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 9

claim: A moxGFP mutant (mox-T203I) has fluorescence reduced to 78% of mox.
source: The fluorescence of this mutant is reduced to 78% of mox (Figure 2—figure supplement 10A–C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10A–C

claim: The mox-T203I mutant has an NI intermediate between mox and mox-YG.
source: The growth rate of the cells expressing this mox-T203I was like that of mox and mox-YG (Figure 2—figure supplement 10E). Still, the expression limit was intermediate between mox and mox-YG (Figure 2—figure supplement 10F), resulting in the NI intermediate between mox and mox-YG (Figure 2—figure supplement 10G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10E–G

claim: The mox-T65S mutant was expressed 12% more than mox.
source: The mox-T65S mutant was expressed 12% more than mox (Figure 2—figure supplement 10H, I)
evidence: Supported by protein quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10H, I

claim: The phenol-type fluorophore can be a limiting factor for the expression level of fluorescent proteins.
source: suggesting that the phenol-type fluorophore can be a limiting factor for the expression level of the fluorescent protein, while the concrete mechanism is still unclear.

claim: The overall trend of expression changes was similar between mox and mox-YG overexpression (r=0.64).
source: The overall trend of expression changes was similar (r=0.64, Figure 3A).

claim: Enhanced ribosome synthesis and decreased glycolysis were observed in mox overexpression.
source: In addition to the enhanced ribosome synthesis and decreased glycolysis observed in previous mox overexpression (Namba et al., 2022)

claim: Enhanced oxidative phosphorylation was detected in mox and mox-YG overexpression.

claim: IFH1 was upregulated in mox but downregulated in mox-YG.

claim: Most of the transcriptional responses observed under mox-YG overexpression were not observed under moxFS overexpression.
source: As a result, most of the responses observed under mox-YG overexpression were not observed under moxFS overexpression, suggesting that these transcriptional responses are likely caused by a burden on translation.

claim: The transcriptional responses in mox-YG overexpression are likely caused by a burden on translation.

claim: Mox-YG overexpressing cells showed reduced ribosome density in the cytoplasm.
source: in addition to reduced ribosome density in the cytoplasm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: Abnormal nucleolar formation in mox-YG overexpressing cells was confirmed by fluorescence microscopy images of Nsr1 (Nucleolin).
source: This abnormal nucleolar formation was also confirmed by fluorescence microscopy images of Nsr1 (Nucleolin), the major protein of the nucleolus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D

claim: Overexpression of mox-YG creates an imbalance between the amount of ribosomal protein synthesized in the cytoplasm and the amount of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesized that overexpression of mox-YG creates an imbalance between the amount of ribosomal protein synthesized in the cytoplasm and the amount of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Hypothesis based on proteome data and microscopy observations

claim: The imbalance between ribosomal protein and rRNA may lead to the creation of misassembled ribosomes, which are eventually degraded.
source: The imbalance may lead to the creation of misassembled ribosomes, which are eventually degraded.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observed imbalance

claim: The primary enzyme degrading the misassembled ribosome should be the nuclear exosome.
source: We speculated that the primary enzyme degrading the misassembled ribosome should be the nuclear exosome.
evidence: Speculation based on previous genome-wide mutation analysis

claim: The mtr4-1 mutant does not show growth retardation upon mox-YG overexpression.
source: We confirmed that the mtr4-1 mutant does not show growth retardation upon mox-YG overexpression (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5E

claim: In mtr4-1 cells, there was no difference in growth rate between the vector control and mox-YG overexpression.
source: In fact, in mtr4-1 cells, there was no difference in growth rate between the vector control and mox-YG overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B)
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B

claim: Mox-YG overexpression restores the effect of growth inhibition caused by mtr4-1.
source: Therefore, in mtr4-1 cells, even though mox-YG overexpression reduced the amount of other proteins (to 54%) compared to the vector control (78%), the growth rate was not reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B). This suggests that mox-YG overexpression restores the effect of growth inhibition caused by mtr4-1.
evidence: Inference from growth rate and protein quantification data

claim: The failure of nucleolus formation observed upon mox-YG overexpression was partially, but significantly, rescued in the mtr4-1 strain.
source: The failure of nucleolus formation observed upon mox-YG overexpression was partially, but significantly, rescued in the mtr4-1 strain.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 5D, E

claim: Mox-YG overexpressing cells stop growth earlier (lower final density) at higher temperatures (38°C) than the vector controls.
source: While experimenting with mox-YG overexpressing cells, we found that these cells stop growth earlier (lower final density) at higher temperatures (38 °C) than the vector controls (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 6A

claim: At 30°C, hyperosmolarity caused the same decrease in growth for the vector control and mox-YG overexpression.
source: At 30 °C, hyperosmolarity caused the same decrease in growth for the vector control and mox-YG overexpression (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 6C

claim: At 38°C, hyperosmolarity caused a decrease in growth only in the vector control and no further decrease in mox-YG overexpression cells.
source: On the other hand, at 38 °C, hyperosmolarity caused a decrease in growth only in the vector control and no further decrease in mox-YG overexpression cells (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: Supported by growth data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 6D

claim: Mox-YG overexpression and hyperosmolarity may mitigate each other's growth-inhibitory effects.
source: This suggests that mox-YG overexpression and hyperosmolarity may mitigate each other's growth-inhibitory effects
evidence: Inference from the observation that hyperosmolarity does not further decrease growth in mox-YG cells at 38°C

claim: Hyperosmolarity may suppress the abnormal organization of the nucleolus caused by mox-YG overexpression.
source: and one explanation may be that hyperosmolarity suppresses the abnormal organization of the nucleolus caused by mox-YG overexpression.
evidence: Speculation based on nucleolus size data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6E, F

claim: The neutrality of Gpm1–CCmut was highest among glycolytic enzymes tested, equivalent to that of mox-YG.
source: The calculated NIs were highest for Gpm1–CCmut, which was equivalent to that of mox-YG (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by neutrality index calculations shown in Figure 6A

claim: The activities of glycolytic enzymes can become constraints in some way.
source: We previously concluded that the activities of glycolytic enzymes generally do not affect their expression limits (Eguchi et al., 2018), but their neutralities suggest that their activities can become constraints in some way.
evidence: Inference from comparison of wild-type and CCmut neutrality indices

claim: Cells overexpressing Gpm1 appeared enlarged and spherical.
source: Cells overexpressing Gpm1 appeared enlarged and spherical
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Cells overexpressing Gpm1–CCmut did not show hypertrophy but were rounder than vector controls or mox-YG overexpressing cells.
source: while those overexpressing Gpm1–CCmut did not show such hypertrophy but were still rounder than vector controls or mox-YG overexpressing cells.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: The transcriptional responses observed in mox-YG overexpressing cells, including the induction of GAP1, were not detected in Gpm1–CCmut overexpression.
source: The transcriptional responses observed in mox-YG overexpressing cells, including the induction of GAP1, a marker of the amino acid starvation response, were not detected in Gpm1–CCmut overexpression (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 4

claim: Mitochondrial development was observed in Gpm1–CCmut cells using Rip1–mScarlet-I labeling.
source: While mitochondrial development was observed in Gpm1–CCmut cells using Rip1–mScarlet-I labeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5

claim: No increase in oxygen consumption was detected in Gpm1–CCmut overexpressing cells.
source: no increase in oxygen consumption was detected (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption measurement data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 6

claim: The nucleolus appeared similarly shrunken in Gpm1–CCmut overexpressing cells as in mox-YG overexpressing cells.
source: The nucleolus, visualized with Nsr1–mScarlet-I, appeared similarly shrunken in Gpm1–CCmut overexpressing cells as in mox-YG overexpressing cells (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 7

claim: The phenotypes observed in mox-YG overexpressing cells include both mox-YG-specific effects and responses commonly associated with protein burden.
source: These results suggest that the phenotypes observed in mox-YG overexpressing cells include both mox-YG-specific effects and responses commonly associated with protein burden.
evidence: Inference from comparison of mox-YG and Gpm1-CCmut overexpression phenotypes

claim: Gpm1–CCmut may possess unknown constraints or cytotoxic properties not captured by the neutrality index.
source: Alternatively, as indicated by the abnormal cell morphology, Gpm1–CCmut may possess unknown constraints or cytotoxic properties not captured by the neutrality index, which could obscure the detection of phenotypes typically associated with protein burden.
evidence: Speculation based on observed differences between mox-YG and Gpm1-CCmut phenotypes
